title: The Operational Tax
description: Confront the hidden costs of microservices: 100 deploy pipelines, contract testing, the integration test pyramid, feature flags, and the monorepo vs polyrepo decision.

segments.text: Nobody talks about this in conference talks, but one hundred microservices means one hundred CI/CD pipelines, one hundred sets of monitoring dashboards, one hundred deployment configurations. At Segment, they famously moved back to a monolith because the operational tax of microservices was crushing their small team.

Each service needs its own build, test, deploy pipeline. Change a shared library? You need to update and redeploy every service that uses it. At Google, they process fifty thousand builds per day through their CI system. Without a platform team automating this, smaller organizations drown.

Integration tests across services are fragile and slow. Contract testing with Pact is the answer. The consumer defines what it expects from the provider — a contract. The provider runs those contracts in its own CI pipeline. If it breaks the contract, the build fails before deployment.

The microservices test pyramid is different from monolith testing. Unit tests are fast, run them extensively. Contract tests replace most integration tests. End-to-end tests should be minimal — maybe five critical user journeys. Google's guideline: seventy percent unit, twenty percent contract, ten percent end-to-end.

Here's the dilemma. You've got twenty teams deploying independently. Team A deploys a breaking change to the user API. Team B's service starts failing in production. Contract tests would have caught this, but they weren't set up. How do you prevent this organizationally?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you enforce API contracts across twenty independently deploying teams?

segments.text: Feature flags enable trunk-based development — everyone commits to main, but new features are wrapped in flags and turned off in production. This eliminates long-lived feature branches and merge conflicts. Deploy daily, release when ready. Netflix runs thousands of concurrent feature flags managed by their internal platform.

But feature flags create technical debt. At one company I worked with, they had three thousand active flags with no cleanup process. Engineers couldn't tell which flags were still needed. Old flags referenced deleted services. You need a flag lifecycle — create, activate, clean up. Set a TTL on every flag, and alert when flags exceed their expiry.

Monorepo versus polyrepo is a religious debate. Google, Meta, and Twitter use monorepos — one repository for all code. Atomic refactoring across services, shared tooling, unified CI. But you need custom build tools like Bazel that understand dependency graphs, or every commit rebuilds everything.

Polyrepo: each service in its own repository. Cleaner ownership boundaries, independent CI pipelines, smaller clone times. But cross-service changes require coordinated PRs. Spotify uses polyrepo with strong service ownership — each squad owns their repos entirely. The trade-off is autonomy versus coordination cost.

Your company has fifty engineers across eight teams, one hundred and twenty microservices, and growing. You're currently using polyrepo and cross-service changes take weeks of coordination. Should you switch to monorepo?
segments.thought_prompt: Monorepo or polyrepo for 50 engineers, 120 services? What factors drive your decision?

segments.text: The operational tax is real and unavoidable. Staff engineers earn their title by managing this complexity: automate CI/CD with templates, enforce contracts with Pact, keep end-to-end tests minimal, use feature flags with cleanup policies, and choose your repo strategy based on team size and coordination needs. Microservices are an organizational scaling tool, not a technical silver bullet.
